section_summary: This section assembles cross-references, correspondence, intelligence memoranda, diplomatic despatches, and reports concerning Japanese industrial capacity and economic mobilization from late 1940 through 1943. Early documents assess raw-material self-sufficiency, American-owned manufacturing in Japan, German industrial participation, aircraft production, labor and transport problems, and specific sugar, phosphate, and copper enterprises. The principal document is a detailed March 1943 report on government industrial controls, wartime investment, metals, electric power, mining, chemicals, synthetic materials and fuels, and land transportation, followed by distribution correspondence and supplementary material on business-asset valuations and the Industrial Bank of Japan.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on the Japanese ten-year self-sufficiency program
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a telegram concerning Japan's policy for achieving economic self-sufficiency across Japan, China, and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram on Japan's basic policy backing a ten-year program for complete self-sufficiency of Japan, China and Manchukuo, filed 894.50/124.

subfiles.title: Letter concerning The Industrialization of Japan and Manchukuo
subfiles.about: Elliott transmits an analysis of E. B. Schumpeter's book and distances himself from its conclusions.
subfiles.summary: Elliott says the enclosed analysis raises points for an introduction he declined to write because he sponsored the book, thinks Schumpeter trusted Japanese sources too much, but hopes the study stays useful to Feis.

subfiles.title: Analysis of Japanese self-sufficiency in major raw materials through 1945
subfiles.about: The memorandum challenges optimistic conclusions about Japan's ability to become self-sufficient in strategic raw materials.
subfiles.summary: Comparing Schumpeter's estimates with other assessments of twenty-six essential raw materials, Japan stayed seriously deficient in fifteen; ferro-alloy self-sufficiency is doubtful, conquest of China or the Indies and a Russian deal could help, and mercury, molybdenum, nitrates, wool, aviation fuel and steel capacity remain weak.

subfiles.title: Report on Nanyō Kōhatsu K.K. (South Seas Development Company)
subfiles.doc_type: industrial intelligence report with administrative cover
subfiles.about: The report describes the sugar, alcohol, phosphate, fiber, and plantation activities of the South Seas Development Company.
subfiles.summary: Nanyo Kohatsu ran sugar plants on Saipan, Tinian and Rota, developed mandate phosphates, held Philippine deposits, grew cotton and hemp in New Guinea and a Celebes coconut plantation; shipping shortages hurt phosphates and a merger with Taiwan Takushoku was expected; pages 8-9 duplicate.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on Japanese industrial-control legislation
subfiles.about: The sheet refers to a telegram about legislation extending rigid Japanese government control over industrial production.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference to a telegram: American-owned manufacturers in Japan worry about new controls, with possible retaliatory U.S. controls on Japanese holdings; file 894.5034/23.

subfiles.title: Duplicate continuation concerning Nanyō Kōhatsu K.K.
subfiles.about: This duplicate report page repeats information about alcohol, phosphate, plantation holdings, shipping difficulties, and a possible merger.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate continuation on Nanyo Kohatsu: Pohnpei alcohol, island phosphates, Philippine, New Guinea and Celebes holdings, shipping shortages and a predicted Taiwan Takushoku merger, repeating pages 8-9.

subfiles.title: Duplicate cross-reference note on Japanese industrial-control legislation
subfiles.about: This second filing copy points to the same telegram on Japanese industrial controls and American corporate concerns.
subfiles.summary: Duplicate cross-reference on industrial-control legislation, noting American manufacturers' anxiety and suggested retaliatory controls on Japanese holdings.

subfiles.title: Industrial conditions in Japan as observed by Mr. Plowman
subfiles.about: Plowman briefs American officials on construction restrictions, manufacturing, labor, shortages, transportation, and public conditions in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Plowman explains that new construction was largely confined to factories and government buildings needed for military purposes, with detailed permits required for every raw material used in elevators. He reports priority bottlenecks, skilled-labor shortages, rapid worker turnover, close police control, and shortages of rice, charcoal, water, power, coal, gas, and transportation. Rail equipment around Tokyo and Yokohama appeared overused and poorly maintained, while the public mood seemed depressed. Otis's Japanese production had fallen to about twenty percent of its former level, although it retained a dominant market share, and Plowman reported only a general impression of German influence rather than direct knowledge of German technicians.

subfiles.title: Instruction transmitting the Plowman memorandum to Tokyo
subfiles.about: The Secretary of State forwards the April 7 memorandum on industrial conditions in Japan for the ambassador's confidential information.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends Tokyo the memorandum of conversation with Plowman, the former Otis manager, a confidential account of Japanese industrial conditions.

subfiles.title: German industrial participation in Japan and Manchukuo
subfiles.from: Sam E. Woods, American Embassy, Berlin
subfiles.about: Woods transmits a German mining-newspaper supplement documenting German exports of industrial equipment to Japan and Manchukuo.
subfiles.summary: A German supplement surveyed German industrial penetration of Japan and Manchukuo through photographs and articles, stressing heavy capital goods, coke ovens, turbines and mining equipment that substituted for foreign exchange; five copies of the April 6 Deutsche Bergwerks-Zeitung supplement enclosed.

subfiles.title: FBI letter transmitting intelligence on Japanese industries and railways
subfiles.about: The FBI sends confidential-source information about Japanese industries and railways to the State Department.
subfiles.summary: FBI letter encloses a December 9 memorandum from a confidential, reliable source on Japanese industries and railways, copied to Naval Intelligence's T. S. Wilkinson and G-2's Sherman Miles.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Japanese aircraft, export industries, labor, and railways
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation confidential source
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports aircraft output, the collapse of export industries, acute skilled-labor problems, and congestion on Japanese railways.
subfiles.summary: Source claims Mitsubishi made thirty-five C-20 transports monthly and Nakajima copied the Hurricane; exports outside occupied Asia ceased, closing factories and idling about 600,000 women; skilled labor went to North China, and railways suffered congestion and breakdowns but could carry essential wartime materials.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on H. U. Pearce's report
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report by former General Electric representative H. U. Pearce on Japanese industrial conditions.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: H. U. Pearce, General Electric's Tokyo representative 1924-1941; original report filed at 740.0011 P.W./1694.

subfiles.title: FBI letter transmitting intelligence on Japanese industrial production
subfiles.about: The FBI forwards an outside confidential-source memorandum concerning industrial production in Japan.
subfiles.summary: FBI sends Berle a confidential, reliable source's information on Japanese industrial production, copied to Rear Admiral T. S. Wilkinson and Brigadier General Raymond Lee.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on decentralized aircraft production and metal shortages
subfiles.from: Federal Bureau of Investigation confidential source
subfiles.about: The memorandum reports decentralized Japanese aircraft-parts production, a purported underground aviation base, scrap-metal reserves, and underperforming Manchukuo plants.
subfiles.summary: Aircraft parts are reportedly dispersed among small factories and assembled at Nagoya, Kobe and Yokohama, with an underground waterfront facility near Mikado Beach; metal shortages cut production about forty-five percent after July 1941, and new Manchukuo plants ran at about forty percent.

subfiles.title: File separator for document 894.60/27
subfiles.about: The page contains only the file designation 894.60/27 and separates the following Montreal despatch.
subfiles.summary: No substantive text appears on this sheet. Its file number corresponds to the despatch and enclosure on pages 30–32.

subfiles.title: Despatch transmitting information on Japanese copper facilities
subfiles.from: Homer Byington, American Consulate General, Montreal
subfiles.about: Byington forwards a confidential memorandum from W. A. Higgins on copper mines, a refinery, and a smelter in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Byington transmits in duplicate Higgins's memorandum on Japanese copper facilities from pre-1927 knowledge; since he may return to Japan after the war, he asks his identity not be linked to it.

subfiles.title: Anonymous memorandum on Sumitomo copper mines, refinery, and smelter
subfiles.about: Higgins describes the locations and estimated capacity of Sumitomo copper operations around Shikoku and the Seto Inland Sea.
subfiles.summary: Higgins locates Sumitomo's Besshi mines, Niihama electrolytic refinery and offshore smelter, estimates ingot copper at no less than 100,000 tons yearly near a triangle formed by Okayama and Kure Naval Base, recalls Japanese police scrutiny and requests anonymity.

subfiles.title: Japanese Wartime Industry
subfiles.from: Roy M. Melbourne, American Consulate General, Istanbul
subfiles.about: The report surveys Japan's wartime system of industrial control and developments in investment, metals, power, mining, chemicals, fuels, and land transportation.
subfiles.summary: Drawing chiefly on material collected by former Argentine special attaché Ramon Lavalle, the report describes nine new control associations and a national program to raise mining, machinery, chemical, and Southern Area resource efficiency. It surveys wartime capital investment, aid to small manufacturers, standardization, conversion of factories, steel and aircraft production, skilled-labor incentives, and severe electric-power and shipping bottlenecks. Further sections examine aluminum and other light metals, tungsten, copper, mercury and asbestos, substitute fibers and chemicals, synthetic rubber, shale oil, lubricants, butanol-based aviation fuel, and fuel derived from rubber. The final section relates industrial output to rail and truck capacity, discusses the Kanmon Tunnel and proposals for unified imperial railway control, and lists commodities receiving transport priority.

subfiles.title: Instruction distributing Istanbul reports to New Delhi
subfiles.to: Officer in Charge, American Mission, New Delhi
subfiles.about: The instruction sends three Istanbul reports for mission files and for representatives of the Board of Economic Warfare.
subfiles.summary: Instruction sends New Delhi Istanbul reports 7, 8 and 11 on Japanese wartime industry, economy, and administration and finance in occupied territories, to be kept and shared with Board of Economic Warfare representatives.

subfiles.title: Department of State memorandum forwarding additions to Istanbul despatch no. 7
subfiles.about: The memorandum records Ramon Lavalle's request that additional items be appended to the Istanbul report on Japanese wartime industry.
subfiles.summary: Memo identifies Lavalle, former Argentine Embassy special attaché who left Tokyo January 9, 1943, as the source of Istanbul despatch 7 and asks inclusion of supplementary material.

subfiles.title: Additions to Japanese Wartime Industry: asset valuation and Industrial Bank dividends
subfiles.about: The addendum describes official valuation rules for people leaving occupations and reports an increased Industrial Bank of Japan dividend.
subfiles.summary: Additions: Commerce and Industry Ministry rules for valuing assets of people changing occupations, with basic assessments for small retailers; and the Industrial Bank of Japan raised its dividend from six to seven percent in August 1942 after cuts since the 1927 panic; a final item continues.
